title: How to verify a resume: employment history, degrees and licences
summary: Job seekers stretch claims more often than they invent them. How to check each claim against a record the candidate did not write, and what a mismatch can mean.
body_markdown:
Break it into separate claims (employers, titles, dates, degrees, licences and projects) and check each one against a record the candidate did not write, such as a company registry, an archived copy of the employer's website, the school's registrar or a licensing board's lookup. Confirm details that are not public, such as employment dates or a transcript, with the employer or school after the candidate has agreed. Then mark each claim as confirmed, explained or open, and ask the candidate about anything that does not match.


The direct route is to ask the former employer to confirm dates and title, with the candidate's consent, through contact details you find yourself. Public records add context: company registries show when an employer was incorporated, archived copies of its website can show the person on a team page, and conference programmes, papers and press releases name people with their employer at a particular date.


Check the company registry for its incorporation date and any former names, look for archived copies of its website in the Internet Archive, and search for talks, papers or press releases that name the candidate with the company. If the company was acquired, the acquirer may be able to confirm dates. Documents the candidate kept, such as an offer letter or a contract, can fill the remaining gaps.


First confirm the school is accredited by a recognised accreditor, using the US Department of Education's DAPIP database or CHEA's database for US schools. Then ask the school's registrar to confirm the degree, with the candidate's consent, and find the registrar through the school's own website, because the FTC notes that some diploma mills run their own fake verification services. For a degree from abroad, CHEA's international directory lists quality assurance bodies and ministries of education around the world.


Stretching a claim is more common than inventing one. In three anonymous surveys published in the Journal of Business and Psychology in 2019, an average of 72 percent of respondents said they had embellished their resume in their current or most recent job search to at least some extent, 61 percent had left relevant information out, and 31 percent had fabricated information.


On its own, no. People take time out to study, care for someone, recover from illness or look for the right role, and none of that has to appear on a resume. Ask what the candidate was doing if they are willing to say, and treat the answer as context.
